pairs.title: Bakery cream cakes
pairs.version_a: Dana worked the closing shift at a bakery. Her manager had told her to put the cream cakes in the fridge before leaving. Dana was tired and wanted to get home, so she left the cakes on the counter overnight. The next morning the shop sold the cakes, and eleven customers got food poisoning. The cream had been fresh when it was delivered, so if the cakes had been refrigerated, they would have been safe to eat.
pairs.version_b: Dana worked the closing shift at a bakery. Her manager had told her to put the cream cakes in the fridge before leaving. Dana was tired and wanted to get home, so she left the cakes on the counter overnight. The next morning the shop sold the cakes, and eleven customers got food poisoning. The cream had been spoiled when it was delivered, so even if the cakes had been refrigerated, they would have made people sick.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether refrigerating the cakes would have prevented the food poisoning (fresh cream) or not (cream already spoiled).
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was it of Dana to leave the cream cakes on the counter overnight?
pairs.comprehension_question: Where did Dana leave the cakes overnight?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers usually rate an act as more wrong when the harm depended on it, though the identical act and knowledge keep the gap modest.
pairs.originality_note: An original food-safety case with its own setting, not a re-skin of any standard vignette.

pairs.title: Hotel bathtub flood
pairs.version_a: Jonas was staying in a hotel. He started filling the bathtub, then went down to the lobby to chat with a friend for an hour, leaving the tap running. The tub overflowed, and water soaked through the ceiling of the room below, ruining its carpet and bed. The pipes in the wall were sound, so without the running tap the room below would have stayed dry.
pairs.version_b: Jonas was staying in a hotel. He started filling the bathtub, then went down to the lobby to chat with a friend for an hour, leaving the tap running. The tub overflowed, and water soaked through the ceiling of the room below, ruining its carpet and bed. A pipe in the wall had a crack, so even without the running tap the room below would have been soaked.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether the room below would have stayed dry without Jonas's running tap (sound pipes) or been soaked anyway (cracked pipe).
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was it of Jonas to leave the bathtub tap running while he went to the lobby?
pairs.comprehension_question: What did Jonas leave running while he went to the lobby?
pairs.prediction_rationale: When the flood was unavoidable, readers tend to soften their judgment of the tap-leaving, but Jonas's careless act stays identical so the effect is moderate.
pairs.originality_note: An original everyday household-damage case with a different harm and setting from the other pairs.

pairs.title: Market lane blocked
pairs.version_a: A town market has a rule: nobody may park a vehicle in the lane behind the stalls before ten o'clock, because the lane is narrow. Tariq, who had read this rule on the market notice board, parked his van in the lane at eight. Later that morning the ice truck, which was allowed to park there, pulled in beside it. Together the van and the truck filled the lane, so the fish seller's cart could not get through, and his fish spoiled in the sun.
pairs.version_b: A town market has a rule: nobody may park a vehicle in the lane behind the stalls before ten o'clock, because the lane is narrow. Tariq, who had never seen this rule on the market notice board and was never told about it, parked his van in the lane at eight. Later that morning the ice truck, which was allowed to park there, pulled in beside it. Together the van and the truck filled the lane, so the fish seller's cart could not get through, and his fish spoiled in the sun.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether Tariq had read the parking rule (A) or had never seen or been told about it (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How much did Tariq cause the fish seller's fish to spoil?
pairs.comprehension_question: What did the ice truck driver's parking do, according to the scenario?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers often credit a rule-breaker who knew the rule with more causal responsibility, though the identical action limits the gap.
pairs.originality_note: An original market-parking scenario unrelated to published rule-knowledge vignettes.

pairs.title: Restaurant water pressure
pairs.version_a: A restaurant has a rule: nobody may run the dishwasher during the dinner rush, because it drops the water pressure. Marcus, who had read this rule on the kitchen wall chart, ran the dishwasher at seven o'clock. A minute later Elena opened the large tap to fill a stockpot, which was allowed. Together the dishwasher and the tap dropped the pressure so low that the steam oven shut off, and dinner service was delayed by an hour.
pairs.version_b: A restaurant has a rule: nobody may run the dishwasher during the dinner rush, because it drops the water pressure. Marcus, who had never seen this rule on the kitchen wall chart and was never told about it, ran the dishwasher at seven o'clock. A minute later Elena opened the large tap to fill a stockpot, which was allowed. Together the dishwasher and the tap dropped the pressure so low that the steam oven shut off, and dinner service was delayed by an hour.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether Marcus had read the dishwasher rule (A) or had never seen or been told about it (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How much did Marcus cause the dinner service to be delayed?
pairs.comprehension_question: What did Elena do at about seven o'clock?
pairs.option_a: Filled a stockpot from the large tap
pairs.prediction_rationale: Knowledge of the rule tends to raise causal ratings of the person who broke it, as in prior work on norm violation and causation.
pairs.originality_note: An original kitchen scenario with a different rule, setting and harm than the other pairs.

pairs.title: Brush fire gust
pairs.version_a: Lena owned a small farm. On a dry afternoon she decided to burn a pile of cut brush near her fence, even though she knew a gust of wind could carry sparks to the dry grass next door. She judged the chance of that to be small and lit the pile. Later a gust of wind blew across the field. The sparks fell on bare dirt and went out, and Lena's neighbor never knew anything had happened. No damage was done.
pairs.version_b: Lena owned a small farm. On a dry afternoon she decided to burn a pile of cut brush near her fence, even though she knew a gust of wind could carry sparks to the dry grass next door. She judged the chance of that to be small and lit the pile. Later a gust of wind blew across the field. The sparks landed in the dry grass and set her neighbor's barn on fire. The barn burned to the ground.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether the gust carried the sparks to bare dirt where they died (A) or to dry grass that burned the neighbor's barn (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Lena's choice to burn the brush that afternoon?
pairs.comprehension_question: What did Lena do on the dry afternoon?
pairs.option_b: She burned a pile of cut brush
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers usually let a bad outcome inflate wrongness ratings even with identical choice and risk, though instructed to judge the choice, so I expect a modest gap.
pairs.originality_note: An original rural brush-burning case, distinct from standard drunk-driving or negligence vignettes.

pairs.title: Skipped wiring test
pairs.version_a: Greg was an electrician replacing an outlet in a tenant's kitchen. To get home earlier, he skipped the final safety test, even though he knew there was a small chance the wiring was faulty. He chose to leave without testing it. That night a storm caused a power surge in the building. The outlet worked normally, and the tenant never noticed anything. No damage was done.
pairs.version_b: Greg was an electrician replacing an outlet in a tenant's kitchen. To get home earlier, he skipped the final safety test, even though he knew there was a small chance the wiring was faulty. He chose to leave without testing it. That night a storm caused a power surge in the building. The outlet sparked and started a fire, and the tenant's kitchen was badly burned.
pairs.intended_difference: Whether the outlet worked normally during the surge (A) or sparked and burned the kitchen (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Greg's choice to leave without doing the safety test?
pairs.comprehension_question: What did Greg skip before leaving?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Outcome bias should make the burned kitchen look like a worse choice even though the choice, knowledge and risk are identical.
pairs.originality_note: An original tradesperson case with its own setting, not adapted from known moral luck vignettes.
